video_title: AI:AM Highlights: Clean Neurons, Black October, the GPU Credit Crunch, and Buying the Supply Chain
gist: Weekly AI-in-the-AM highlights: Zvi Mowshowitz on RSI timelines, interpretability hype and Anthropic's leaked federal AI bill; SF Compute's Evan Conrad on GPU credit as the true buildout bottleneck; and Cambrian's atoms-over-bits supply-chain thesis (memory, wafers) against Elon-style disruption risk.

insights.claim: Zvi argues the Romer-style analysis (RSI fizzles without new paradigms or scaling laws) is probably true but irrelevant, because paradigm 'home runs' do occur and must be included in expectations.
insights.speaker: Zvi Mowshowitz (guest)
insights.so_what: Treat 'RSI peters out' models as a floor case, not a forecast; keep fat-tail acceleration in AI-capex and risk scenarios.
insights.quote: It's like, you know, well, here's how many touchdowns, here's how many points we expect to score in this game if nobody ever hits a home run

insights.claim: Exponential growth in tokens used per person and lines of code committed is already visible at Anthropic and OpenAI, and Nvidia published evidence that the time to double CUDA efficiency shrank dramatically during 2026.
insights.speaker: Zvi Mowshowitz (guest)
insights.so_what: Non-lab evidence (a hardware vendor) of AI-accelerated R&D; watch kernel/compiler efficiency gains as an RSI indicator.

insights.claim: Zvi says people he trusts across OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind and METR expect 2027 to be 'completely crazy' and 2028 possibly unrecognizable, and that slow-takeoff-style RSI has already begun at a low level.
insights.speaker: Zvi Mowshowitz (guest)
insights.so_what: Lab-insider consensus pegs the steepest change in 2027-28; position horizons for capex, labor and policy shocks accordingly.

insights.claim: If nothing slows labs down, model release cycles could compress from two months to one month to two weeks to a week, and the current path looks 'eerily' like the AI 2027 scenario.
insights.speaker: Zvi Mowshowitz (guest)
insights.so_what: Faster release cadence shortens the shelf life of any AI-moat or benchmark-based valuation thesis.
insights.quote: We are kind of on an AI 2027 style timeline right now.

insights.claim: Zvi says the pace of AI news already forces him to triage: stories that would have been major six months ago now get a sentence or are dropped, and this will worsen by mid-2027.
insights.speaker: Zvi Mowshowitz (guest)
insights.so_what: Information overload is itself a signal of acceleration and an edge for those with good filters.

insights.claim: Goodfire's essay claims individual neurons mostly do one understandable job, implying earlier messiness was a 'skill issue' of weaker models and tools; Nathan sees real substance but not a new era.
insights.speaker: Nathan Labenz (host)
insights.so_what: Interpretability progress is incremental; don't price it as solving the alignment bottleneck.

insights.claim: Backprop-free training that focuses guesses on strongly activated neurons reproduces gradient updates almost exactly, but remains slow and uncompetitive with backprop.
insights.speaker: Nathan Labenz (host)
insights.so_what: Watch for non-differentiable architectures; today it is research-only, not a threat to GPU-backprop demand.

insights.claim: Zvi says the essay was dramatically oversold: weak activations, the cache and attention remain unexplained, and it cannot predict or explain what a network will output; the highlighted 'Colorado' neuron also responds to tornado systems.
insights.speaker: Zvi Mowshowitz (guest)
insights.so_what: Discount hype from OpenAI-side reactions; interpretability still can't support strong safety assurances.

insights.claim: The main barrier to interpretability was brute force (too many neurons, too little compute), so the problem is perhaps '10 times easier' than thought, which Zvi frames as roughly a year's head start rather than a fundamental change.
insights.speaker: Zvi Mowshowitz (guest)
insights.so_what: Compute scaling also scales interpretability; the gain is real but modest.

themes.theme: Model awareness of monitoring and training interventions

insights.claim: An independent researcher showed models can be trained to detect internal activation probes via GPU floating-point ordering effects; Zvi calls it a valid existence proof and says anything an AI can be trained to do, it eventually will be.
insights.speaker: Zvi Mowshowitz (guest)
insights.so_what: Monitoring-based safety evals will degrade as models get harder to fool; raises tail-risk and compliance-cost assumptions.
insights.quote: anything that an AI can be trained to do, it will be trained to do at some point down the line

insights.claim: Zvi warns that optimizing a network's internals to look good to interpretability tools is 'playing with liquid fire' because it trains the model to hide what you don't want to see, while also potentially boosting capabilities.
insights.speaker: Zvi Mowshowitz (guest)
insights.so_what: Interpretability-guided training is both a capabilities lever and a safety hazard; a signal for regulatory scrutiny.

themes.theme: Cognitive core vs. big world-knowledge models

insights.claim: Zvi rejects the Karpathy 'cognitive core' idea (small reasoning model plus retrieval): memorized facts and linked intuitions drive effectiveness, and the break-even for how much a model should memorize keeps rising as compute gets cheaper and algorithms improve.
insights.speaker: Zvi Mowshowitz (guest)
insights.so_what: Argues large frontier models keep their edge over small local models; supports continued demand for scale.

insights.claim: A pure cognitive core would be amoral because values like 'don't steal' are injected as context, so the same core could be loaded with the opposite values.
insights.speaker: Zvi Mowshowitz (guest)
insights.so_what: Small stripped-down models raise misuse and alignment concerns that large aligned models partly mitigate.

themes.theme: Black October: AI-era cyber risk to banks

insights.claim: Two critical PHP bugs were disclosed with millions of exploit attempts already counted by Cloudflare, and an 'OpenAI/Hugging Face' breach involving ~1,200 agent traces was cited as an example of AI-enabled attacks.
insights.speaker: Nathan Labenz (host)
insights.so_what: Cyber-security demand tailwind; also tail risk for any internet-facing financial infrastructure.

insights.claim: Pash argues the FDIC can sustain a bank with untrusted records by honoring checks and withdrawals on promises and clawing back overdrafts later, so a records-destroying attack would still be contained and the government would over-compensate to avoid runs.
insights.speaker: Pash (co-host)
insights.so_what: Systemic bank-failure risk from cyberattacks is backstopped by the state; moral hazard rises.

insights.claim: Nathan doubts the FDIC's Friday-to-Monday resolution playbook generalizes when balance-sheet records themselves can't be trusted, e.g. when agents falsify logs.
insights.speaker: Nathan Labenz (host)
insights.so_what: Resolution regimes were built for credit losses, not data-integrity failures; a gap worth watching.

insights.claim: Pash says the endgame for authentication is network-level identity, since users can't be expected to hold keys worth millions; the cost is the end of digital anonymity.
insights.speaker: Pash (co-host)
insights.so_what: Supports identity/biometric-authentication themes; privacy trade-off.
insights.quote: it's anonymity only to the extent that network wants to preserve your anonymity

insights.claim: Nathan argues cyber security will not be a major AI-created jobs boom, because firms will spin up agents to supervise agents instead of running hiring processes.
insights.speaker: Nathan Labenz (host)
insights.so_what: Counter to the 'AI creates cyber jobs' narrative; favors automation vendors over labor-heavy security services.

themes.theme: GPU credit as the compute bottleneck

insights.claim: Evan Conrad says the binding constraint on AI buildout is not power or chips but credit, because lenders can't underwrite GPU-cluster collateral and so rely on the customer's credit quality.
insights.speaker: Evan Conrad, SF Compute CEO
insights.so_what: GPU-backed debt pricing and availability is the lever; track CoreWeave-style debt costs.
insights.quote: right now the bottleneck in compute and AI in general is not power, it's not um chips. Uh it's entirely credit.

insights.claim: Lenders and clouds want investment-grade customers like Meta or Google, so non-IG AI labs must pay big deposits or long 3-5 year contracts, explaining astronomical pre-revenue funding rounds as survivorship bias.
insights.speaker: Evan Conrad, SF Compute CEO
insights.so_what: Capital access, not merit, selects which labs survive; consolidation pressure favors hyperscaler-adjacent players.

insights.claim: SF Compute is trying to make GPU collateral valuable via a liquid resale market, but says it will take several years because lenders only build comfort over long proof periods.
insights.speaker: Evan Conrad, SF Compute CEO
insights.so_what: A liquid GPU resale/futures market is a prospective fix; early-stage and unproven.

insights.claim: Evan says neocloud prices are not meaningfully below hyperscalers; the gap is on-demand vs. reserved pricing, with hyperscaler on-demand priced high to cover idle capacity.
insights.speaker: Evan Conrad, SF Compute CEO
insights.so_what: Compare like-for-like contract types when judging neocloud pricing power.

insights.claim: SF Compute uses Harberger-style (Henry George) pricing so capacity buyers must allow others to buy part of it, discouraging hoarding and keeping it unsold-out while 'every GPU cloud is sold out'.
insights.speaker: Evan Conrad, SF Compute CEO
insights.so_what: Market design that boosts liquidity; a model for scarce-compute allocation.

insights.claim: Evan claims his prediction of a credit crunch within three months was almost exact: CoreWeave debt is getting costlier, non-IG customers are hard to close, and many are asked for 100% upfront payment.
insights.speaker: Evan Conrad, SF Compute CEO
insights.so_what: Credit-tightening signals in neocloud financing; relevant for neocloud credit and equity risk.

insights.claim: Evan expects a year or two of AI lab and inference-company consolidation, with companies unable to prepay clusters being forced to sell to high-credit buyers, so VCs should be ready to write big checks or encourage sales.
insights.speaker: Evan Conrad, SF Compute CEO
insights.so_what: M&A into big-tech balance sheets; startup concentration risk.
insights.quote: we're going to probably see a lot of consolidation of AI labs and inference companies

themes.theme: Atoms over bits: AI supply-chain thesis

insights.claim: Cambrian's thesis is that physical suppliers (memory, wafers, fabs, capacitors) will capture more AI value than designers like Nvidia, Broadcom, Arm and Marvell, because labs can design chips but never replace a wafer maker.
insights.speaker: Lonus, Cambrian managing partner
insights.so_what: Disclosed bias: Nathan has committed to invest in Cambrian. Supplier moats are decades of tacit know-how.

insights.claim: Lonus says semis trade at ~16x earnings versus ~22x for the S&P and ~40x for Walmart, and wafer, memory, capacitor and foundry names at 3-5x sales, implying the market sees AI-driven earnings as less durable than average.
insights.speaker: Lonus, Cambrian managing partner
insights.so_what: Valuation gap is the core of the long-supply-chain trade.
insights.quote: I mean, if you look at how these semi stocks are are trading, they're trading at 16 times earnings or so.

insights.claim: Public AI exposure is under-priced because few Wall Street investors are 'AI-pilled', whereas private-market buyers (ex-operators) bid startups to 50-100x sales.
insights.speaker: Lonus, Cambrian managing partner
insights.so_what: Mispricing is structural to who owns public equities.

insights.claim: The steelman: these suppliers are poor businesses in normal conditions (high fixed costs, debt, ~10% gross margins), but a 10% price rise doubles earnings and doubled prices 10x them, so the thesis only works if AI demand truly hits.
insights.speaker: Lonus, Cambrian managing partner
insights.so_what: Operating leverage makes this a levered bet on AI demand; downside if demand disappoints.

insights.claim: On memory, Lonus says no expert with a track record thinks DRAM bit supply can exceed ~2.5x by decade end, and that at 5-6x earnings it only needs rerating to 10-12x; bits per token fell ~500x from GPT-3 to DeepSeek V4 while DRAM bit prices rose 6-7x.
insights.speaker: Lonus, Cambrian managing partner
insights.so_what: Memory pricing thesis; main risk is faster-than-expected memory compression.
insights.quote: nobody thinks we can 3x that's like zero experts

insights.claim: Energy is less likely than semis to be the bottleneck because power has latent supply (behind-the-meter gas, repurposed truck and aircraft engines despite turbines sold out to 2030), whereas wafers and memory have no slack.
insights.speaker: Lonus, Cambrian managing partner
insights.so_what: Supports semis over power as the scarcer resource; the bear case is power becoming binding again.

insights.claim: Lonus argues LLMs will design chips (Anthropic-Micron and OpenAI-Synopsys/Cadence ties were cited) long before they can build fabs, since tacit knowledge in veteran engineers lacks training data, unlike bio.
insights.speaker: Lonus, Cambrian managing partner
insights.so_what: Chip design is exposed to AI first; manufacturing moats persist for longer.
insights.quote: it's a very significant difference between designing a ship and and producing the ship

insights.claim: Pash argues Elon Musk can break supply bottlenecks because he gambles huge capital (like in launch, where he holds ~90% of commercial capacity and ~99.9% after Starship), unlike risk-averse suppliers such as ASML; only RSI-driven superintelligence from Anthropic or OpenAI stops that outcome.
insights.speaker: Pash (co-host)
insights.so_what: Key bear risk for supplier thesis: a well-capitalized vertical integrator in semis.

insights.claim: Pash's 'adversarial diffusion' theory says 10-20% GDP growth only occurs under emergencies like wars or COVID (mRNA), so AI adoption may arrive via cyber and bio crises with matching politics.
insights.speaker: Pash (co-host)
insights.so_what: Political backlash is the biggest risk to the bottleneck thesis.

insights.claim: Nathan sees a narrow path to pausing frontier hyperscaling for a cycle without popping the bubble, since adoption of current models has far to go, though a government attempt could go wrong.
insights.speaker: Nathan Labenz (host)
insights.so_what: Policy-induced capex slowdown is a tail scenario for AI infrastructure.

insights.claim: A leaked Anthropic-written draft federal AI bill (similar to June's Frontier Act) trades transparency rules for preempting state AI laws; Zvi says it would nullify state laws immediately while implementing new requirements months later, and it uses weak burdens such as judicial review before any model takedown.
insights.speaker: Zvi Mowshowitz (guest)
insights.so_what: Federal preemption fight is a live regulatory risk for labs; watch for a Congress vote.

insights.claim: Zvi says preemption can only be traded once, so passing a weak bill would make a stronger one harder next Congress; Pash counters that Congress moves fast when scared and ad hoc government action should be formalized.
insights.speaker: Zvi Mowshowitz (guest)
insights.so_what: Order of legislation matters for how strict future AI regulation gets.

insights.claim: Zvi says labs themselves see a coming crisis, perhaps in 2027, where capabilities outpace alignment, forcing a choice between commercial viability and catastrophic or loss-of-control risk, and policy must 'meet the moment'.
insights.speaker: Zvi Mowshowitz (guest)
insights.so_what: Lab-acknowledged risk raises odds of tougher regulation.

insights.claim: Zvi rates Anthropic as the most responsible lab but 'grading on a curve', arguing its policy division and competitive behavior (buying capacity, encouraging chip and power supply) make it act like a normal corporation.
insights.speaker: Zvi Mowshowitz (guest)
insights.so_what: Anthropic's policy positioning is a reputational and regulatory variable.

insights.claim: Nathan runs a split agent setup, a high-access/low-autonomy laptop agent and low-access/high-autonomy Mac Mini agents, with a rule that no agent gets both, plus an approval step for sensitive outbound data that causes alert fatigue after ~5 false positives.
insights.speaker: Nathan Labenz (host)
insights.so_what: Practical agent-security design; alert fatigue is the main failure mode.

insights.claim: Nathan is building 'Helper' (HelpPier), a protocol for personal agents to cooperate with friends' agents on behalf of their humans, since no established pattern exists for cross-person agent networks.
insights.speaker: Nathan Labenz (host)
insights.so_what: Early signal of agent-to-agent networking demand.
